books.subtitle: A Code of Conduct for Programmers in the Age of AI Agents
books.author: Anuj Sadani
books.desc: A field guide for the working engineer when a stochastic, non-deterministic teammate writes a substantial fraction of the code — and the human at the keyboard still owns every commit that ships under their name. An updated professional ethic for the agent era: the orchestrator role, verification duty, provenance as part of the artifact, and concrete practices you can apply on Monday. A chapter-for-chapter response, fifteen years on, to The Clean Coder.

digital.title: The Meter Is Not the Money
digital.desc: Everyone calls tokens the currency of AI, including the chief executive who justified buying a router with the line. Every credit balance in the market is denominated in dollars instead — because providers serving the identical open-weight model differ threefold in price, the router picks between them with a weighted draw so the cost of a request is a distribution rather than a number when you press send, and writing to a cache can cost more than an ordinary input token with the sign of the adjustment varying by vendor. A token is a meter reading, not a unit of account; every credit is a conversion layer over dollars; the position worth owning is the exchange desk rather than the mint. Includes the strongest case against that argument, presented without rebuttal.

digital.title: A Monolith Wearing a Transformer
digital.desc: A payments company announced a transformer trained on four billion transactions, and a research document proposed that routing, fraud, risk and checkout all be served from it — specifying an inference budget of 29 milliseconds, cited four times, that appears in none of the company's own materials. This paper takes the architecture seriously anyway. Service boundaries were blast-radius machinery: a shared backbone removes the compartment the bulkhead pattern exists to create, which makes its failure a single point of failure by construction rather than by misconfiguration. Nobody has benchmarked the thing being argued about. A domain foundation model is a strong supporting system and a poor primary one.

digital.title: Onboarding Slop
digital.desc: Onboarding a new engineer quietly became a link to a knowledge base and a link to an assistant — ask it anything. The feedback loop that would catch the cost is broken in a known direction: two unrelated studies found what people report about an AI tool comes apart from what measurement shows they learned, and the error favours whatever felt smoothest. The studies that test understanding run for an hour; the ones that run for weeks count merged code; nothing occupies the space between. The mistake is not adopting AI. It is adopting autonomy.

digital.title: Speed Is the Moat
digital.desc: Once token cost is understood, the claim goes, inference speed is the next durable advantage. It isn't — speed is a lead with a half-life of one to two months, with inference software delivering up to 2x more throughput on unchanged silicon inside a single month. What survives is narrower: latency is a priced contract term, not an engineering win. The cover states the proposition; the book is the audit.

digital.title: Abundant and Uncurated
digital.desc: Machine judgement already beats human annotation on accuracy and cost, so the case for keeping people in the loop cannot rest on being better. A model that verifies its own synthetic data plateaus at what it already knows, and evaluation criteria cannot be fixed before you look at the outputs. Machines apply judgement; humans form the criteria and supply the signal from outside the system. Every claim bound to a quoted source, including the two that failed.

digital.title: The Human Leverage Map: Finding Durable Human Value When Intelligence Becomes Abundant
digital.desc: When intelligence becomes abundant and cheap, judgment becomes scarce. A two-axis map for finding the human value that survives AI: where your leverage goes when the machine can produce the answer, how that leverage collapses without anyone noticing, and how to defend the faculty it depends on. The full designed PDF.

digital.title: The Engineers Who Didn't Make It Through AI
digital.desc: Twelve brilliant principal engineers made rational decisions based on the world they knew, then the world changed faster than their optimization function. The Craftsman, the Skeptic, the Lone Expert, the Builder: twelve failure modes of senior technical leadership during a discontinuity, braided into one argument. A companion to Three Leaders, One Market, turned on people instead of firms. No villains, only people who optimized for a reality that stopped existing.

digital.title: The Monk Who Oversold the AI
digital.desc: Why borrowed foundation-model capability is shared capability — how a product leader scales on it for two years and still dissolves the only moat the product had.

digital.title: Three Leaders, One Market: A Field Report on Why Good AI Strategies Still Fail
digital.desc: A field report on good-faith failure: three experienced leaders, three defensible AI strategies in one market, and why all three fail as the market keeps moving what it rewards.

digital.title: The Barbell & The Vanishing Middle: IDP
digital.desc: Where intelligent document processing is heading through 2028 — value migrating to infrastructure and decision automation while the extraction middle becomes invisible, not simple.
